common_name: Mutabilis Rose (Butterfly Rose, Color-Changing China Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or grafted plants in spring after hard frost, or in fall in mild-winter climates; Mutabilis is an antique China rose first recorded in cultivation in 1894, exceptionally heat- and humidity-tolerant, and one of the most reliable roses for the Gulf South where many modern roses struggle with blackspot.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil enriched with compost, spacing plants at least 4-5 feet apart to allow for its eventual size, since Mutabilis can grow into a large, airy shrub 6-8 feet tall in warm climates over several years. Known as the Butterfly Rose for the way its single, five-petaled blooms seem to flutter above the foliage, Mutabilis opens flame-yellow, ages through pink, and finishes deep crimson, so a single established bush displays all three colors at once. As a China rose it blooms almost continuously from spring through frost with little deadheading required, and it is exceptionally resistant to blackspot and powdery mildew, making it one of the most reliable antique roses for the hot, humid Gulf South. It tolerates poor soil and some drought once established but flowers best and grows most vigorously with regular water and an occasional feeding. Prune lightly in late winter only to shape and remove dead wood, since Mutabilis flowers on both old and new growth and heavy pruning sacrifices bloom.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Earth-Kind Rose Trials

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Caldwell Pink is a 'found rose' rescued from an old Texas homestead by rose rustlers, and its polyantha vigor and disease resistance make it one of the toughest small shrub roses for the humid Gulf South.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, spacing plants 2-3 feet apart for a dense flowering hedge or mass planting. Caldwell Pink is a 'found rose' — a once-common variety that fell out of the nursery trade but survived for decades at an old homesite before being rediscovered, propagated, and named by Texas rose rustlers for the town of Caldwell, Texas, where it was found. It produces a profusion of small, fully double, medium-pink pompon blooms in dense clusters nearly continuously from spring through fall, on a compact, well-branched polyantha shrub. It is extremely disease-resistant and largely free of the blackspot and mildew problems that plague many modern roses in humid climates, needing no spraying and very little care beyond an annual light shaping. Established plants tolerate considerable drought and heat, making Caldwell Pink one of the most reliable low-maintenance flowering shrubs for Gulf Coast gardens.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Earth-Kind Rose Trials
The Antique Rose Emporium — Found Rose Collection
American Rose Society — Polyantha Class Descriptions

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Marie Pavié is an 1888 French polyantha valued in Gulf South gardens for its strong sweet fragrance, compact habit, and outstanding resistance to blackspot and powdery mildew.

directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained, compost-enriched soil, spacing plants 2-3 feet apart. Introduced in France in 1888, Marie Pavié is a classic polyantha prized for producing dense clusters of small, fully double, blush-pink-to-white blooms with a strong, sweet fragrance unusual for such a compact rose. The tidy, rounded shrub blooms in flushes nearly year-round in mild climates and shows outstanding resistance to blackspot and powdery mildew, requiring little to no spraying even in the humid Gulf South. Its modest size and dense, twiggy habit make it well suited to borders, low hedges, and containers, and it tolerates part shade better than most roses, though flowering is heaviest in full sun. Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead or crossing wood and to maintain shape; deadhead spent clusters to encourage continued rebloom.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Earth-Kind Rose Trials

common_name: Mrs. B.R. Cant Rose (Antique Southern Tea Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Mrs. B.R. Cant is an 1901 tea rose long grown in Deep South cemetery and homestead gardens for its vigor, heat tolerance, and near-total immunity to the blackspot that plagues modern roses in humid climates.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, allowing 3-5 feet between plants since this vigorous tea rose can reach 6-8 feet in warm climates over time. Introduced in 1901 and named for the wife of an English rose nurseryman, Mrs. B.R. Cant became a mainstay of Deep South gardens and old cemeteries because of its extraordinary heat tolerance, vigor, and near-total resistance to blackspot, which lets it thrive in the humid Gulf South with no spraying. Large, cupped, silvery-pink double blooms with a rich tea fragrance appear in flushes from spring through the first frost, most heavily in cooler weather. Like most tea roses, it prefers to be left largely alone — minimal pruning beyond removing dead or damaged wood keeps the plant blooming reliably, since heavy pruning delays flowering and reduces the shrub's naturally graceful, arching form. Established plants tolerate considerable drought and neglect, which is why so many survive today in abandoned Southern homesites decades after they were planted.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Earth-Kind Rose Trials
The Antique Rose Emporium — Tea Rose Collection
American Rose Society — Historic Tea Rose Class

common_name: Belinda's Dream Rose (Texas A&M Earth-Kind Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall; Belinda's Dream was bred in Texas and named an Earth-Kind rose by Texas A&M AgriLife for its outstanding heat tolerance and disease resistance without spraying, making it one of the most widely recommended shrub roses for Gulf Coast gardens.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, compost-enriched soil, spacing plants 3-4 feet apart for good air circulation. Bred by Texas hobbyist Mike Shoup in 1988 and later designated an Earth-Kind rose by Texas A&M AgriLife Extension after years of trial evaluation, Belinda's Dream combines the large, fully double, clear-pink, classically shaped blooms and strong fragrance of a hybrid tea with the toughness and disease resistance of an antique shrub rose. It flowers in repeated flushes from spring through frost and shows outstanding resistance to blackspot even in the humid Gulf South, requiring no fungicide spraying under the Earth-Kind trial protocol. The upright, well-branched shrub works equally well as a specimen, in mixed borders, or massed as an informal hedge, and its blooms hold up well as cut flowers. Prune back by about a third in late winter to encourage vigorous new flowering wood, and deadhead spent blooms through the season to keep the shrub reblooming steadily.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Earth-Kind Rose Trials
